raw_output.title: Cash-Flow Forecasting for First-Time Agency Owners

slides.title: Your agency looks profitable. So why is your bank account empty?
slides.body: Revenue and cash are not the same thing. Most first-time agency owners learn this the hard way. Here's how to stop the panic and start forecasting.

slides.title: Cash-flow forecasting is not accounting. It's a survival tool.
slides.body: Accounting tells you what happened. Forecasting tells you what's coming. You need to know — 8 weeks from now — whether you can make payroll, pay contractors, and keep the lights on.

slides.title: Start with your 'cash-in' calendar, not your invoices.
slides.body: List every client. Note when they actually pay — not when you invoice. Net-30 clients who pay on day 45 are a cash-flow problem hiding in plain sight. Date of deposit is what matters.

slides.title: Map your fixed cash-out dates with the same precision.
slides.body: Payroll, software subscriptions, rent, contractor minimums — list them by the exact date they leave your account. You're building a 60-day picture of cash in versus cash out, week by week.

slides.title: The 'danger gap' is the week your out-dates beat your in-dates.
slides.body: Every agency has one. It usually falls at the end of a month before retainer payments clear. Name your danger gap. Know its size. That number is what your operating reserve must cover.

slides.title: A simple forecast beats a complex spreadsheet you never open.
slides.body: Use a single tab: dates down the left, projected in, projected out, and running balance. Update it every Friday. Fifteen minutes a week will catch problems 30 days before they become crises.

slides.title: Three levers when your forecast turns red: speed, delay, or bridge.
slides.body: Speed up collections — send invoices earlier, offer 2% early-pay discounts. Delay non-critical spend. Or bridge the gap with a line of credit you set up before you need it, not after.

slides.title: Build your forecast this weekend. Your future self will thank you.
slides.body: Download a free agency cash-flow template in the link below. Takes 90 minutes to set up, saves you from scrambling for cash at the worst possible time. Follow for more no-fluff agency finance.

test_case.input: Build a concise carousel for experienced product managers showing how to distinguish a weak customer signal from repeatable evidence. Include practical tests, avoid buzzwords, and end with an action the reader can take this week.
test_case.expected_behavior: Address experienced product managers with practical evidence tests, avoid buzzwords, and finish with an immediate action.

raw_output.title: Weak Signal or Real Evidence? A PM's Field Test

slides.title: One customer complaint isn't a roadmap item.
slides.body: Experienced PMs know the danger: a loud voice in a user interview shapes the next sprint. Here's how to tell the difference between noise and a pattern worth acting on.

slides.title: What makes a signal weak?
slides.body: A signal is weak when it comes from one source, surfaces under leading questions, or disappears when you change the framing. Enthusiasm in a demo is not validation.

slides.title: The repetition test
slides.body: Has the problem appeared unprompted across at least five separate conversations — different segments, different contexts? If you had to fish for it, it doesn't count.

slides.title: The specificity test
slides.body: Vague pain is cheap. Ask: can the customer describe the last time this cost them time, money, or a decision? Concrete recall is a stronger indicator than general frustration.

slides.title: The behavior test
slides.body: What are people doing right now to work around the problem? Workarounds — spreadsheets, Slack bots, manual exports — are evidence. 'We'd probably use that' is not.

slides.title: The consistency test
slides.body: Run the same core question through three different formats: interview, support ticket review, and usage data. If only one format surfaces the problem, treat it as a hypothesis, not a finding.

slides.title: This week: audit your top three backlog items
slides.body: Pick three items sitting near the top of your roadmap. Write down which test each one passes. If an item fails two or more, move it to a discovery column before it blocks real work.
